title: Herro Says Harris Likes Japan, Credit Suisse and UBS: Video
description: Feb. 17 (Bloomberg) -- David Herro, chief investment officer for international equities at Harris Associates LP, talks with Bloomberg's Margaret Brennan about his investment strategy including Japanese stocks and European banks. (Source: Bloomberg)

asr.full_text: What to Japanese companies which have been dealing with a weak domestic economy Luxury good companies which have been hit by cutdowns in consumer spending and troubled automaker Toyota Which has been plagued by recent? controversy have in common All Morningstar's international stock fund manager of the decade has found reasons to like them. That's David Hero he's chief investment officer of international equities and portfolio manager at Harris Associates THEY GET ON THEIR STORES ON WHITE STOCKS, IT IS A BAD DAY AND THEY ARE STILL BORING AND THEY DON'T LIKE THEM. THAT'S DAVID, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER OF INTERNATIONS EQUITIES AND PORTFOLIO MANAGER AT HARRIS ASSOCIATES. HE JOINS US NOW THAT LIFE FROM CHICAGO. DAVID, YOU HAVE GOT A LET OF REALLY COUNTER INSTINCTIVE CALLS, HERE AND I FIND THEM VERY INTERESTING, HERE, TELL ME WHY ARE YOU FINDING REASONS TO PUT MONEY TO WORK IN JAPAN RIGHT NOW? to put money to work in Japan right now. One of the secrets I think to successful long-term investing is to look for the true values, and where the true values are usually is where the momentum is not. And if you take the Japanese market, it hit a peak in December 31, 1989, it is steadily IT HAS BEEN THIS WAY TOGETHER WITH A PREVIOUS CONDITIONS FORECAST, JUST AT THE END OF THE 18-19, 2021, IT IS STEABLING FALLING SINCE THEN WITH LITTLE FITS AND RECOVERIES BUT, TODAY, WE SEE GOOD UNDERLYING LOW PRICED STOCKS BUT WE ALSO SEE CORPORATE BEHAVIOR THAT IS EVER-SOME SLOWLY CHANGING IN FIRMS OF MAKING COMPANIES MORE PROFITABLE AND MORE SHAREHOLDER FRIENDLY, THIS WE JUDGE BY JUST LOOKING AT RETURNS AND SO THE DEMOCRATS HAVE LID FOR GENERAL PROBLEMS WITH THE EQUITY OF THE ECONOMY AND THE FUTURE OF THE ECONOMY ARE MORE SHAREHOLDER FRIENDLY, AND THIS WE JUDGE BY LOOKING AT RETURNS AND CAPITAL ALLOCATION OF POLICIES. NOW, WHEN JAPAN IS REFERENCED THESE DAYS, IT IS TYPICALLY AS SORT OF A WARNING FOR WHAT MAY COME HERE IN THE U.S., THE THE SPEAR OF A LOST DECADE PEOPLE WORRY ABOUT WITH LACK OF ECONOMIC GROWTH, BUT WHAT YOU ARE SAYING IS YOU ARE MAKING THIS CALL AND PUTTING MONEY TO WORK IN JAPAN you're saying, it sounds like to me is that you are making this call on putting money to work in Japan based on valuations, not necessarily on economic robustness there. Yes, what you have to look at is how that macro-economy of a local economy impacts a company's ability to generate cash flow for its owners. And often, especially if it is a company that has heavy outside of Japan or heavy external sales and profits, it has very little impact. So investors often get confused with what's happening in a macroeconomy with the intrinsic value of the underlying security itself. And this is the imperfection which we, one of the imperfections we try to exploit as long-term investors. Now I'm looking at AROUND FALL. SO, THERE'S A PEOPLE THERE. ALL OF THIS STUCK. AND ONE OF THE IMPERFECTIONS WE WANT TO IMPROVE WERE TRY TO EXPLOIT IS LONG-TERM INVESTORS. I'M LOOKING AT OAK MARK INTERNATIONAL FUND. ONE OF THE FUNDS HERE. FOUR BILLION THERE. ONE YEAR RETURN. 61% OUT-PERFORMING. 96% OF ITS PEERS. INTERNATIONAL STOCKS, SO MUCH INTEREST IN THE EMERGING MARKETS BUT YOU ARE ACTUALLY UNDERWEIGHT THE BRICK COUNTRIES, BRASIL, CHINA, RUSSIA, INDIA? WHY ARE YOU UNDERWEIGHT THE BRICKS? BECAUSE OUR INVESTMENT CRITERIA IS BASED NOT ON WHO HAS THE FASTEST GROWING ECONOMY, BUT WHAT ARE THE BEST-QUALITY COMPANIES SELLING AT THE LOST PRICES. THAT IS OUR VALUE PROPOSITION. AND, AGAIN, LIKE I SAID EARLIER, INVESTORS SOMETIMES GET CONFUSED AND WE DON'T LOOK AFTER A SHELTER IN TERMS OF OUR LOSS PRICES. THERE IS VALUE PROPOSITION. LIKE I SAID EARLIER INVESTORS SOMETIMES GET CONFUSED BELIEVING THAT JUST BECAUSE THERE IS FAST GROWTH MEANS THERE IS AN AVAILABILITY AND VALUE IN FACT OFTEN THIS IS JUST THE OPPOSITE. THE GROWTH GETS OVERLY BIKED IN TO THE SHARE PRICES THEREBY MAKING THEM UNATTRACTIVE AND IN THE CASE OF THE BRITK'S THEDUSTRIES THAT HAVE THE RESTLESSES, THEY'RE BY MAKING THEM UNATTRACTIVE. AND IN THE CASE OF THE BRICS, THE COUNTRIES THAT YOU MENTIONED, THIS IS MOSTLY THE CASE. WHEN I LOOK AT YOUR ALLOCATION ON A GEOGRAPHIC BASIS OF YOUR FUNDS, YOU'RE MORE HEAVILY WEIGHTED TOWARDS SWIZERLAND, THE UK, FRANCE AND GERMANY, THAN THOSE TYPICAL INTERNATIONAL NAMES THAT ARE SO OFTEN BANDIED ABOUT. TELL ME, THOUGH, LOOKING AT WHAT I think these are very important problems that we've talked to often bandied about. Tell me though, looking at what we have seen in the past few weeks with weakness in the euro, would you put money to work in the financial sectors of Europe, into European banks? It's really on a case-by-case basis. The banks that we have investments in, some of the big Swiss private banks such as Credit Suisse, UBS, have, have very large and profitable asset management divisions which we find very attractive. UBS is more of a turnaround story but we do believe that the turnaround at UBS is well underway, and though it doesn't look like it in a very short-term over the medium and long term, we're going to see asset inflows back into that private bank. There are some commercial banks we like in Europe as well. BNP, Bank of Ireland is a turnaround story. But we wouldn't necessarily just do a huge basket. It's a stock-by-stock specific story. All right. David, I know you also like some luxury names, Richemont, Signet Jewelers among them. Thank you so much for this counter call. We appreciate it.
